Yes, the .303 is a perfect example of a cartridge that would hugely benefit as well as saving significant money. Many surplus SMLE rifles have excessive headspace problems, and brass will stretch excessively at the web on first firing. After that, the brass will last a lot longer if you neck size only and only use those cartridges in that rifle. With .303 (as well as 8mm Mauser) you should be checking brass after every firing for imminent case head separation.

Absolutely, have your rifle's head space checked by a competent gunsmith. .303 surplus rifles (as well as surplus 8mm Mauser) are notorious for this. At first firing the brass undergoes excessive web stretching, as well as blown primers and stretched primer pockets from the head not being fully supported. This is a very unsafe condition and should be corrected before using the firearm. Hot high pressure gas in your face and shrapnel in your eyes is some pretty serious shit, and your rifle doesn't like it either.

It's easy to check for this if you have some brass fired in that rifle. First, examine the primer. It shouldn't be backed out, flattened, or pierced. The shouldn't be any soot or other signs of leakage around the outside of the primer, and the primer should retain a visible radius around the edge.

Next, examine the body above the case head for a bright ring. Many cases will show signs of this and still be fine (I have some .30-30s that look like that) but when it's bad it really stands out. Take a paper clip and straighten it out, then put a 90 degree bend in one end with some pliers. Use this feeler tool to "scratch" up and down inside the case where the ring is. You can feel the thinning in this area if it's excessive.

7mm TCU, a .284 bullet in a 5.56 case. This was from my first efforts to use range pick up, before I learned how to anneal. This case neck expanded without splitting (I was losing over 25% just neck expanding alone) but the brittle brass couldn't stretch anymore during the seating process and failed in two ways at the same time. I still managed to get 50 loaded, but lost almost all of them on first firing to shoulder or neck splits.

Then I learned how to anneal, and all the problems disappeared. I have formed over 1000 random cases since then, and loss rate at forming/loading went to zero, with about a 2% loss at fire forming due to mouth cracks. Even these would load one more time, but would split at the next firing so I toss 'em. I then anneal these newly fire formed cases one more time and they're good to go. I now anneal all my bottleneck cases, and have noticed that full length sizing seems easier, and especially neck expanding.

tl;dr Learn to anneal, your brass with thank you for it.
